title: EU rejects Trump’s case for new tariffs
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday rejected Washington’s claim that Europe is fueling global industrial overcapacity, after the Trump administration proposed a 15% tariff on the 27-country bloc.

“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Olof Gill, the Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson, said in a statement. 

“The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” he added. 

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, led by Jamieson Greer, found that 14 trading partners, including the European Union, China and Japan, had artificially deflated prices by flooding markets with manufactured goods. The decision follows a trade investigation launched in March.

Greer on Wednesday proposed a 15% tariff on the European Union, in line with the ceiling agreed in the transatlantic trade truce struck in July 2025 between U.S. President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

title: Parliament clears 7 EU budget files for negotiations
content:
The European Parliament voted by large majorities to send seven proposals for the EU’s next long-term budget straight into negotiations with the Council, heading off a possible challenge from the far right.

The lawmakers were voting on the proposals for Global Europe, the European Social Fund, Horizon Europe, the Connecting Europe Facility, the European Competitiveness Fund, the asylum and migration program and AgoraEU. 

These proposals are now moving to negotiations with the Council of the European Union based on reports adopted by the committees responsible for each file.

creator: Aude van den Hove

title: EU Commission wants €50B fund to keep tech European
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission is planning to take direct stakes worth hundreds of millions of euros in homegrown tech companies to keep them European, according to a plan unveiled Wednesday.

The Sovereign Tech Equity Fund has an envisioned size of €50 billion. Public money from the EU, member countries and partners such as the European Investment Bank will aim to draw in private capital to invest in critical technologies.

The goal is to fund tech that is essential to the bloc’s “technological sovereignty and economic security,” a Commission official told reporters, granted anonymity to discuss details of the plan ahead of its formal presentation.

“We need to use public funding more efficiently as a catalyst to crowd in private capital,” the official added.

The announcement comes two weeks after the EU leaders’ first-ever meeting on AI, where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised to come up with a funding proposal for the EU to become less reliant on U.S. or Chinese technology. The broader investment plan would need about €500 billion, according to Commission estimates.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The European Commission is planning to take direct stakes worth hundreds of millions of euros in homegrown tech companies to keep them European, according to a plan unveiled Wednesday.
creator: Pieter Haeck

title: Quantum may be a bigger security risk than AI. Europe’s got a plan.
content:
BRUSSELS — As the world seeks a way through a wave of AI-powered cyberattacks and rogue agents, the next security threat already looms: quantum technology. 

With quantum computers set to break long-established protocols for securing digital information and communications in everything from messaging to banking services, their deployment in the next few years will spark a new security scramble.

The EU is hoping to get ahead of the risks with a Quantum Act rolling out Wednesday, which aims to secure the bloc’s digital infrastructure, according to a draft obtained by POLITICO.

Even as AI has helped to disrupt services from supermarket fridges to the European Commission’s own platforms over the past month, computer scientists contend that another, potentially more perilous moment for cybersecurity is on the horizon: Q-Day.

The fear is that quantum computers, which can process more than the classic 0s and 1s used by today’s machines, will eclipse current security vulnerabilities by breaking the standard methods of encryption that scramble information in order to lock it down — rendering everything from secure government systems to hospitals digitally defenseless.
snippet: BRUSSELS — As the world seeks a way through a wave of AI-powered cyberattacks and rogue agents, the next security threat already looms: quantum technology.
creator: Pieter Haeck

title: Snowden on steroids: AI agents in phones trigger surveillance fears
content:
AI agents are lurking in your phone, hoovering up your messages, pictures and emails in a privacy breach that “makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke,” privacy proponents are warning.

Privacy-preserving messaging app Signal has started blocking screenshots by default in an attempt to stop AI agents from reading people’s screens and capturing potentially sensitive data.

The makers behind Signal — which is considered the industry gold standard for confidential, encrypted messaging — warned that Google, Apple and Microsoft are integrating autonomous agents “deep” within their device operating systems, allowing the agents to bypass privacy safeguards in individual apps.

“The ability for billions of devices to permanently spy on their users makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke,” Udbhav Tiwari, head of strategy and global affairs at Signal, told POLITICO, referring to the 2013 disclosures about mass U.S. government surveillance.

Tiwari warned that governments with a penchant for surveillance could ask tech firms for access to data gathered by AI agents, skipping the need to break end-to-end encryption or install malware on someone’s device.
snippet: AI agents are lurking in your phone, hoovering up your messages, pictures and emails in a privacy breach that “makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke,” privacy proponents are warning.
creator: Ellen O'Regan

title: Merz to meet Pope Leo, Meloni in Rome
content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will meet Pope Leo XIV and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Monday, three officials familiar with the plans told POLITICO.

The visit to the Vatican, Merz’s first private audience with the pope, is set to focus on human dignity, artificial intelligence and efforts to bring peace to Ukraine, two of the officials said.

Merz also plans to meet Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s top diplomat, who in September used his U.N. General Assembly speech to call for an immediate ceasefire in Ukraine and a path to diplomacy.

A German government spokesperson declined to comment, saying the chancellor’s trips are announced on the Friday of the preceding week.

Merz, a Catholic, attended Leo’s inauguration in May 2025 but did not meet the pontiff in private. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met Parolin at the Vatican in early October for talks that also covered AI, the war in Ukraine and Black Sea grain exports.
snippet: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will meet Pope Leo XIV and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Monday, three officials familiar with the plans told POLITICO.
creator: Hans von der Burchard

title: Right-wing revolt threatens to bog down EU budget
content:
BRUSSELS — The far-right Patriots for Europe group plans to challenge the European Parliament’s negotiating mandates on several files in the EU’s next budget, according to four EU officials with knowledge of the discussions — a move that could drag out discussions on the seven-year plan in the chamber.

The challenge would stop the files, which have already been discussed at a committee level, from going straight to talks with national governments. Instead, the mandates would need a plenary vote, opening the door to amendments that could rehash positions committees had already settled.

“The merger of several programs [in several budget proposals] is accompanied by an increasing concentration of allocation authority in the hands of the Commission,” a PfE official told POLITICO. Moreover, most of the PfE’s amendments in the budget have been rejected, they said.

The official added that “several delegations outside of the PfE” have told them they would support the challenge.

creator: Martina Sapio, Aude van den Hove

title: ‘It’s just a circus’: Founders clash with notaries over new EU startup law
content:
BRUSSELS — Europe’s plan to help startups compete with Silicon Valley has hit an obstacle in the continent’s most buttoned-up profession: notaries.

Unveiled in March as Europe’s answer to Delaware, the European Commission’s EU Inc. proposal would give new companies a quick way to set up a single EU legal entity, sparing them legal advice and form filling in multiple countries. It would also cut notaries out of key stages in a company’s life cycle, a move that has excited startups and rankled the profession.

“It’s just a circus,” said Mihai Streza, a Berlin-based entrepreneur, who sees hefty notary bills and mandatory in-person appointments as emblematic of what Europe gets wrong about startups.

Pushback by the notaries, however, is now complicating negotiations over the proposed regulation, which would create a single company form allowing startups to register online within 48 hours for €100. EU leaders set the end of this year as the deadline for a political deal, but talks between the Parliament and EU countries have yet to start.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Europe’s plan to help startups compete with Silicon Valley has hit an obstacle in the continent’s most buttoned-up profession: notaries.
creator: Jacob Parry

title: Global left rallies in Paris to make ‘not so radical’ case for taxing billionaires
content:
PARIS — The left wants voters to know there is nothing radical about taxing billionaires.

“Radical would be cutting their heads off. But we are not proposing that,” former Chilean President Gabriel Boric told a summit against “international oligarchy” in Paris on Saturday. A minimum tax on the world’s largest fortunes, he said, is “arithmetic.”

Boric was among the left-wing politicians, union leaders and economists brought together by French economist Gabriel Zucman at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue within sight of the U.S. embassy and a short walk from the Elysée. 

The gathering drew lawmakers from the U.S. Congress and opposition leaders from Italy, Germany, Britain and the Netherlands, united in the belief that taxing the super-rich could help the left regain the political initiative.

Their pitch was that Zucman’s proposed annual minimum tax of 2% on billionaires’ wealth is a modest measure that most voters already support — and a potent answer to the far right.

“It’s the status quo which is radical,” said Zucman, who cites polls that put support for his tax in France at 86%.
snippet: PARIS — The left wants voters to know there is nothing radical about taxing billionaires.
creator: Jacob Parry, Sofiane Zaizoune

title: Effort to regulate ‘killer robots’ delayed to 2028
content:
U.N. talks on regulating AI-powered killer robots ended without a negotiating mandate Saturday, as countries decided to extend discussions until 2028.

It’s a result that NGOs called “disappointing.”

Countries party to the U.N.’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons spent five days in Geneva trying to reach an accord to elaborate legally binding rules for weapons that can select and attack targets without human approval.

But resistance from several countries, and especially Russia, blocked those efforts. In the end, the 128 member countries agreed to launch “the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems,” over the next two years, Julien Thöni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the talks, told reporters.

The issue is of growing importance as AI gains new capabilities and autonomous systems become increasingly powerful. Ukraine, Russia, Israel and others are using drones and robots in warfare, although they insist that humans still have ultimate control over pulling the trigger.

However, Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of more than 300 organizations, said such systems have already been tested or deployed, including in Ukraine and Gaza.
snippet:
U.N. talks on regulating AI-powered killer robots ended without a negotiating mandate Saturday, as countries decided to extend discussions until 2028.

It’s a result that NGOs called “disappointing.”
creator: Sérène Nourrisson

title: Costa cuts proposed EU budget by €44B
content:
BRUSSELS — António Costa aims to shave another €44 billion off the EU’s planned seven-year budget, according to a fresh set of numbers unveiled on Saturday.

For the first time since the budget negotiations began last year, EU regional spending, known as cohesion policy, is a target for reductions. The European Council president proposed reducing it by €8 billion compared with the last proposal, while farmers’ subsidies remained untouched.

This is a major setback for a coalition of 17 countries from Eastern and Southern Europe — including Poland, Italy and Spain — who rejected potential cuts to cohesion policy only a few days ago. However, the plan was welcomed as “a first step” by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who urged further cuts.

“This proposal is fit for tackling the challenges we are facing in our societies, and gives the European Union the necessary capacity to act,” Costa said on Saturday morning.
snippet: BRUSSELS — António Costa aims to shave another €44 billion off the EU’s planned seven-year budget, according to a fresh set of numbers unveiled on Saturday.
creator: Gregorio Sorgi

title: French billionaire hunter takes fight global after California tax defeat
content:
PARIS — Gabriel Zucman wants to put the world’s billionaires on notice.

The 40-year-old French economist, who has spent more than a decade designing ways to tax the ultra-rich, hosts a summit against “international oligarchy” in Paris on Saturday. It comes less than three weeks after California voters rejected a billionaire tax he backed, in a campaign where Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other opponents spent more than $300 million to thwart the initiative.

“Everywhere, we see very, very strong popular support for taxing billionaires,” Zucman told POLITICO this week, arguing that his loss in California was only a minor setback. “That’s true even in the United States.”

Zucman sees fresh hope in the results of the U.S. midterms, in which a string of Democrats campaigning to tax the ultra-rich won their races.

“Now our party has a choice to make: Are we going to stand with the working class or the tech lords?” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is flying in for the Paris gathering. “The same inequality is fueling anger and distrust not only in America, but also in France and around the world,” he told POLITICO.
snippet: PARIS — Gabriel Zucman wants to put the world’s billionaires on notice.
creator: Jacob Parry, Sofiane Zaizoune

title: Germany says investors ready to spend €25B to buy TikTok Europe
content:
BRUSSELS — The German government has found investors interested in investing as much as €25 billion to buy the majority of TikTok’s EU operations, Berlin’s culture minister Wolfram Weimer told reporters on Friday.

“We have spoken to a lot of investors already,” he said. “It’s a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business. And TikTok Europe should be open to sell 75% to 80% of the shares.”

Germany and Austria floated the Trump-style initiative earlier this week, citing concerns about TikTok’s influence on European democracy.

A TikTok spokesperson Friday dismissed the push as “nonsense,” saying the company is “already subject to comprehensive European law, including the Digital Services Act and the GDPR, which provide clear legal frameworks for any company investing and operating in Europe.”
snippet: BRUSSELS — The German government has found investors interested in investing as much as €25 billion to buy the majority of TikTok’s EU operations, Berlin’s culture minister Wolfram Weimer told
creator: Eliza Gkritsi

title: How to watch the UK-EU summit like a pro
content:
BRUSSELS — Andy Burnham has gone big on Britain’s relationship with the EU during the first months of his premiership.

By the weekend, he may actually have something to show for it.

The British prime minister is heading to Brussels on Friday for his first U.K.-EU summit. But on the eve of the meeting, what exactly he’ll be coming back with is still up in the air. 

POLITICO analyzed leaked draft communiqués and spoke to diplomats and officials on both sides of the talks to piece together how the agreements are shaping up — and what’s still to be decided.  

Here’s what you need to know.

The U.K. and EU have committed to holding annual summits to build on the relationship they were left with after Brexit.

This is the second such meeting, and is primarily about concluding negotiations on agreements announced at the first gathering back in May 2025.  

That summit was attended by then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer. This week’s meeting was originally due to be held in July, but it was postponed after Starmer stepped down — to give Burnham time to put his stamp on the process.

Three new international agreements are set to be announced at the meeting.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Andy Burnham has gone big on Britain’s relationship with the EU during the first months of his premiership.
creator: Jon Stone, Sophie Inge, Caroline Hug, Mathieu Pollet

title: Costa eyes tax on Big Tech to boost EU budget after Trump’s poor midterms showing
content:
BRUSSELS — António Costa is seizing on an enfeebled Donald Trump to explore levying a tax on U.S. digital giants to finance the EU’s next seven-year budget.

The European Council president is considering asking governments to back a tax on tech companies such as Google and Meta to boost the EU’s approximately €2 trillion budget and unlock a deal on its final size, according to four EU diplomats and officials. In the past years, there has been little appetite for such a tax in Europe for fear of retaliation from Washington, but the Republicans’ poor showing in elections earlier this month appears to have opened the possibility.

“The probability of trade threats from the Trump administration has been reduced after the results from the midterms,” said Siegfried Mureșan, the budget negotiator for the center-right European People’s Party.

Costa, who is due to present a revised budget proposal for 2028-2034 on Saturday, is pushing leaders to agree on it by the end of this year — before votes in France, Italy and Poland threaten to disrupt negotiations.
snippet: BRUSSELS — António Costa is seizing on an enfeebled Donald Trump to explore levying a tax on U.S. digital giants to finance the EU’s next seven-year budget.
creator: Gregorio Sorgi

title: The web is held together by volunteers. AI could tear it apart.
content:
BRUSSELS — Long before the fresh spate of hacks and website shutdowns, the inherent instability of the web was depicted in an internet-famous cartoon of a rickety tower propped up by a single small block.

Now a near-daily rhythm of outages suggests the supporting block may have come loose.

POLITICO revealed Thursday that internal services at EU institutions had gone offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack. That came after service interruptions at U.S. national security offices and the federal aviation authority, global outages at Microsoft and a succession of internet-activated attacks on supermarket refrigerators in Europe.

Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them.

Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated.

creator: Sam Clark

title: Startups call on Commission to salvage or scrap EU Inc proposal
content:
HELSINKI — The European Commission should withdraw and resubmit its proposal for a new EU-wide corporate law framework, startup lobby groups said, denouncing the current text as a “Frankenstein” proposal.

A position on the law adopted by EU capitals in October “weakened or removed some of the very provisions that would make EU Inc. a true European standard,” Startups for Europe and EU Inc. said in a joint press release.

Both groups pitched the withdrawal to European Commissioners Henna Virkkunen and Ekaterina Zaharieva, who oversee tech policy and startups, during a policy roundtable at Finnish technology conference Slush on Thursday morning.

They also sent a joint letter to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen earlier this week.

The European Commission published its proposal for a so-called 28th regime, also known as EU Inc., earlier this year, to harmonize how founders can incorporate a company and reward their personnel, so that startups can scale more easily across the bloc.

The scheme was seen as a challenge to the U.S. state of Delaware, which is known for its flexible incorporation laws.
snippet: HELSINKI — The European Commission should withdraw and resubmit its proposal for a new EU-wide corporate law framework, startup lobby groups said, denouncing the current text as a “Frankenstein”
creator: Pieter Haeck, Jacob Parry

title: Why depth beats breadth in Europe’s hunt for an AI edge
content:
​​​An artificial intelligence (AI) system is judged on the job it does, not on how clever it is in general. For European businesses, that is an opening. For example, a pharmaceutical company does not need a model that can discuss biology. It needs one that can flag the rare adverse-event signal in its own trial data. An energy grid operator needs load forecasts built on its own network topology, not generic ones. A defen​s​​​e manufacturer needs a system that can verify a weld against its own specification, and say why it passed or failed. Each needs a system that understands its domain, works on its data, follows its rules and guardrails, and can be trusted to execute in a protected, controlled environment.

An edge Europe can’t buy

title: Grand Theft Auto VI is here. The EU has 6 reasons to pay attention.
content:
BRUSSELS — Gamers of the world will be taking the day off Thursday to play Grand Theft Auto VI, billed as the most anticipated digital entertainment launch in history. The EU’s buttoned-down staffers may be too busy to notice.

Yet even a diligent Brussels bureaucrat has reason to buckle up for the latest installment of the Grand Theft Auto series, which comes 13 years after the previous version of the controversial video game that challenges players to go on crime rampages around U.S. cities to the tune of an eclectic soundtrack.

According to Sensor Tower data, GTA VI is already the biggest entertainment launch ever, with 17 million copies sold for a total of $1.6 billion (€1.46 billion) before it’s even released.

The game lands in a vastly different world than the one the previous version entered in 2013, one where EU regulators are trying to protect kids from harmful online content and handle the onslaught of AI. Here are six reasons an EU policy maven should pay attention to all the fun and games:

title: EU Commission accused of withholding emails on killing patent law
content:
LUXEMBOURG — The European Commission was accused Wednesday of withholding internal messages that explain why it dropped a contentious patent proposal, amid claims of pressure from U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

At a court hearing in Luxembourg, judges were told that German center-left MEP Tiemo Wölken asked the Commission for internal notes on why the proposal was abruptly killed in early 2025. He was told there was only one relevant internal document: minutes of a private meeting between heads of cabinet, which the Commission refused to hand over.

Wölken’s lawyers said the absence of information was hard to believe given how contentious the proposal had become.

It was “unbelievable” that there were “zero emails on this highly-politicized, economically-relevant procedure,” Carsten Zatschler, Wölken’s lawyer, said at the EU’s General Court.

“All of this apparently happened without any form of electronic communication,” Zatschler said. “That’s quite simply not credible.”
snippet: LUXEMBOURG — The European Commission was accused Wednesday of withholding internal messages that explain why it dropped a contentious patent proposal, amid claims of pressure from U.S. Vice President
creator: Mari Eccles

title: Germany, Austria demand TikTok’s European platform be sold to owners in EU
content:
Germany and Austria say Chinese-owned TikTok should come under European ownership to safeguard personal data, boost sovereignty and curb the platform’s “openly visible threat to our democratic society.”

The joint proposal Wednesday by top government ministers of the two countries comes after President Donald Trump forced the separation last year of TikTok’s operations into a U.S.-based entity, with its original owner, Beijing-based Bytedance holding about one-fifth of the new entity.

Trump’s campaign to initially ban and later split up TikTok cited national security concerns. Now, Berlin and Vienna are going down a similar route.

With 200 million EU users, TikTok is “a central player with significant relevance for opinion formation and social participation,” Germany’s media minister Wolfram Weimer and Austria’s State Secretary for Digitalization, Alexander Pröll said in a joint statement.

A TikTok spokesperson said there was “zero merit” to the proposal.

The platform’s role in elections is being investigated under the EU’s Digital Services Act, while regulators have fined the firm for sending Europeans’ data to China, in breach of privacy rules.
snippet: Germany and Austria say Chinese-owned TikTok should come under European ownership to safeguard personal data, boost sovereignty and curb the platform’s “openly visible threat to our democratic
creator: Eliza Gkritsi

title: Dutch resist ‘unacceptable’ US bid to tighten semiconductor export controls
content:
BRUSSELS — The Netherlands has pushed back against a U.S. congressional bid to tighten restrictions on exports of advanced chipmaking equipment to China, warning that Washington’s attempt to dictate the rules for Dutch companies such as ASML is unacceptable.

The Dutch objections come as the proposed MATCH Act gains fresh momentum in Washington following revelations about Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang and his links to a suspected Chinese spy, intensifying concerns in Congress about Beijing’s access to advanced U.S. technology.

The bipartisan legislation would give U.S. allies, including the Netherlands and Japan, 150 days to align restrictions on sales and servicing of advanced chipmaking equipment to China with those imposed by Washington, or show progress toward doing so. If they fail to comply, the U.S. Commerce Department would be required to extend American export controls unilaterally to equipment supplied from those countries.

“The main concern is the bill’s extraterritorial character,” a spokesperson for the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs told POLITICO on Tuesday.

title: EU Commission eyes rule change to retaliate faster against China
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission is considering changes to its trade enforcement rules that would allow Brussels to respond more swiftly to serious economic threats as it develops a new instrument aimed primarily at China.

The EU’s Enforcement Regulation already allows the bloc to impose countermeasures when trade disputes get stuck in the World Trade Organization’s appeals court. The rule was revamped in 2021 when the court stopped working after Washington blocked appointments of new judges.

Now Brussels is exploring whether the regulation could be tweaked again to allow a broader, quicker response to actions by trading partners that harm EU interests, three people with knowledge of the talks, granted anonymity to discuss the confidential deliberations, told POLITICO.

The work follows a request last month by France and Germany for a new “second strike” tool that would allow the bloc to address economic threats more promptly and effectively.

Other names are being considered for the new instrument, as the bloc wants to ensure it doesn’t borrow from nuclear jargon and draws attention instead to its responsive nature.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The European Commission is considering changes to its trade enforcement rules that would allow Brussels to respond more swiftly to serious economic threats as it develops a new instrument
creator: Camille Gijs

title: Irish regulator stops X training AI with data gathered by agents
content:
Ireland’s privacy regulator has forced X to stop feeding AI models with data collected by its agents, the authority told POLITICO.

The social media giant owned by Elon Musk has suspended the use of so-called third-party data collected by its Grok Bot AI agent, which started mining this data in late October to train its AI systems.

The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) raised “significant concerns” about that data processing in recent weeks, Commissioner Dale Sunderland told POLITICO in an interview. “We asked them to suspend the processing, and they’ve confirmed to us today that they’ve done that,” he said Monday.

X did not respond to a request for comment.

The Irish privacy authority is the most powerful in Europe, as it enforces Europe’s data protection rulebook on companies that have their regional headquarters in Ireland, including Apple, Google, Meta, X and OpenAI.

The X action is a test case as privacy regulators shift their focus from AI training that uses data people have shared about themselves, to third-party data that personal AI agents are accessing and gathering on other people.
snippet: Ireland’s privacy regulator has forced X to stop feeding AI models with data collected by its agents, the authority told POLITICO.
creator: Ellen O'Regan

title: What the EU can learn from Mark Carney on digital sovereignty
content:
At Davos earlier this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney offered a compelling response to a world increasingly shaped by great-power rivalry. Middle powers need greater strategic autonomy, he argued, but they cannot secure it by retreating behind their borders.

Instead, they need to build their own capabilities while working more closely with like-minded partners. On technology, he reasoned that countries should cooperate so they are not ultimately forced to choose between “hegemons and hyperscalers.”

At the recent EU-Canada Summit, that philosophy began to translate into policy. Canada and the EU launched an “Alliance for the Future” based on closer economic, technological and strategic cooperation. They also concluded negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement designed to support a “secure, open and trusted digital environment”​ resilient economic relations​,​ and trusted cross-border data flows.

That principle matters not only for Europe’s new relationship with Canada, but for its approach to other trusted partners.

Sovereignty without isolation

title: Google says Russian speakers pulled off first-ever fully automated AI cyberattack
content:
Russian-speaking hackers built an AI agent that carried out what may be the first-ever fully-automated cyberattack, Google reported Monday.

The tech giant’s cyber threat intelligence division said it had spotted hackers using artificial intelligence to “fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.”

The development could mark an inflection point in the use of AI for cyberattacks, which has dominated headlines and worried policymakers since AI firm Anthropic released its specialized model Mythos in April. 

Hackers, who used Russian in technical documentation identified by Google, set up a series of AI agents to “continuously compare pre- and post-patch code, identify vulnerabilities, and automatically develop exploits without human intervention,” Google said.

That means the agents independently found software flaws and ways to use them. The attackers targeted French websites in the media, entertainment and education sectors, Google said.
snippet: Russian-speaking hackers built an AI agent that carried out what may be the first-ever fully-automated cyberattack, Google reported Monday.
creator: Sam Clark

title: EU sanctions Russian trolls, hackers
content:
European Union member countries on Monday issued sanctions against a Russian company running disinformation campaigns and one of Russia’s most well-known hacking groups.

The Council of the EU said it had sanctioned the Social Design Agency, a Moscow-based firm that carries out “large scale information manipulation and interference projects,” as well as 24 of its staff members.

The Social Design Agency is “funded, directed and supervised” by the Russian government and has organized disinformation campaigns targeting EU countries, EU institutions and European support for Ukraine, Council said.

The group has been connected in the past to a vast online disinformation network known as Doppelganger. It targeted the 2024 European elections and carried out “dedicated operations against EU member states such as Germany and France,” countries said.

EU capitals also agreed to levy sanctions against notorious Russian hacking group NoName057(16), which has targeted government bodies and critical infrastructure as well as private firms in the EU, Ukraine and the United States.
snippet: European Union member countries on Monday issued sanctions against a Russian company running disinformation campaigns and one of Russia’s most well-known hacking groups.
creator: Sam Clark

title: Estonia has a plan for Russian occupation: Run its government from the cloud
content:
TALLINN — Imagine French General Charles de Gaulle, exiled in London during World War II, running his Free France government by logging into the cloud.

Officials in Estonia are preparing for exactly such a scenario with a new strategy to boost doomsday resilience — hukukindlus in Estonian — that would allow the government’s digital services to be run entirely from abroad if its territory is occupied by a foreign enemy.

The Baltic country of  1.3 million, which shares a 294-kilometer border with Russia, fears it is a prime target if Moscow were to invade a European Union country. Security services have already warned that Russia is waging a hybrid war on Europe, and Estonia has blamed Moscow for everything from cyberattacks to arson plots to cuts to undersea data cables.

Now, Tallinn is preparing to move its public services to the cloud “either when data centers are destroyed or there’s boots on the ground and we cannot operate,” said Tõnu Grünberg, an architect of the new strategy and former deputy secretary general for digital infrastructure and cybersecurity at Estonia’s Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs.

title: The EU has always found a way through. On AI, it’s struggling to see it.
content:
There might be an AI apocalypse. European leaders don’t really want to talk about it.

By SEBASTIAN STARCEVIC and PIETER HAECK
in DUBLIN

Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

The European Union wasn’t set up to deal with challenges as vast and existential as the possibility of AI wiping out humanity.

For two decades, the EU’s leaders have muddled through crisis after crisis — from Greece coming within days of being pushed out of the eurozone, to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which forced millions to seek safety in the bloc. Each time, it has found a way through. It’s what the EU does.

With AI, though, it’s turning out to be different.

Tech experts, industry and even governments themselves describe paralysis, distraction and defeatism in Europe’s capitals. It’s telling that it took four years after the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 for EU leaders to bring themselves to discuss artificial intelligence at a summit in Dublin on Friday.

And even then, there was little enthusiasm for the topic.

title: Italy hits Meta with €805M fine over privacy law violation
content:
Italian authorities fined Facebook’s parent company Meta €805 million for using photos and videos from Android phones without users’ specific consent, the Italian Data Protection Authority said in a statement Saturday. 

The fine concerned the “camera roll suggestions when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from a phone’s gallery for users to add to posts.

The feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said. It is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.

The investigation, launched in 2025, established that access to a user’s camera roll is requested with a single permission for the entire app, which the authority said covers multiple features with different needs. The authorization request was preceded by a generic warning that didn’t allow users to understand that they were authorizing picture and video suggestions, the authority said. 

“If granted in full, this type of permission allows the app to read the device’s entire photo archive, usually permanently, without the user or the authorities being able to verify which information is actually being used,” the statement reads.

title: EU deal on Ukraine talks overshadows AI-focused summit in Dublin
content:
They came to discuss AI, but EU leaders spent most of their time during a summit in Dublin on Friday grappling with questions about Ukraine — namely who should represent them in future peace talks.

Despite plenty of disagreement about whether it should be a single person (and if so, who) or a collection of them, they managed to strike a deal: Future talks would involve national security officials from Germany, France, the U.K., Italy and Poland — the so-called E5 powers — plus representatives from the European Commission and European Council. A classic European compromise.

“It is essential to have a team and to speak with one voice,” European Council President António Costa said after the summit, noting that Donald Trump had also tasked two envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with conducting negotiations.

Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency and hosted the informal gathering, had billed the meeting as a rare chance for a high-level discussion on how to develop artificial intelligence in accordance with European values.
